overview.title: Segmenting the mango from a box, and chapter 11 summary
overview.subsection: 11.3.5 Prompting the model with a target box
overview.main_topic: Finishing the box-prompted SAM call, showing the segmented mango (Figure 11.15), noting SAM's value for dataset annotation, and summarising chapter 11.
overview.central_idea: A box prompt is passed under the "boxes" key with shape (1, 1, 2, 2) and yields a clean mask of the mango; SAM can therefore accelerate the creation of segmentation datasets. The chapter's lessons: segmentation means pixel-level masks; you can build a Conv2D/Conv2DTranspose model yourself or use a pretrained promptable model like SAM.
overview.importance: Last content page of chapter 11. It completes the SAM workflow (both prompt types) and condenses the chapter into three takeaways before chapter 12 turns to object detection.
learning_objectives: Explain the "boxes" input and why expand_dims uses axis=(0, 1).
Read Figure 11.15 and compare the mask with the box.
Explain how SAM can speed up dataset annotation.
Recall the three chapter-summary points and where each was developed.

summary:
The page finishes the listing begun on p.351. The input dictionary now has only two keys: `"images"` (the padded image with a batch axis) and `"boxes"`, built with `ops.expand_dims(input_box, axis=(0, 1))`. Expanding along two axes turns the (2, 2) corner array into shape **(1, 1, 2, 2)**: batch of 1, one box per image, two corners, (x, y). No points or labels are supplied. The first candidate is extracted with `get_mask(outputs, 0)` and drawn together with the image and the red box.

**Figure 11.15, "Segmented mango"**, shows the result: the blue mask covers the mango and stops at its outline, even though the box also includes parts of the apples and the bowl. The box only indicated roughly where and how big the object is; SAM found the object's exact pixels.

The authors then make a practical observation: **SAM can be a powerful tool to quickly create large datasets of images annotated with segmentation masks.** This echoes how SA-1B itself was built in a model-in-the-loop process (p.343-344).

The chapter **Summary** has three bullets:

1. Image segmentation is one of the main categories of computer vision tasks; it computes segmentation masks describing image contents at the pixel level (11.1, p.332-334).
2. To build your own segmentation model, stack strided `Conv2D` layers that compress the image into a smaller feature map, then corresponding `Conv2DTranspose` layers that expand it back into a mask of the same size as the input (11.2, p.338-341).
3. You can also use a pretrained model: Segment Anything, available in KerasHub, which the book says supports image, text, point and box prompting (11.3). Only point and box prompts were actually covered in the chapter (see review flag).

paragraphs.excerpt: SAM can be a powerful tool to quickly create large datasets of
paragraphs.what_it_says: SAM can be used to rapidly produce large image datasets annotated with segmentation masks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Hand-drawing pixel masks is slow. With SAM, an annotator only clicks a point or drags a box per object and corrects mistakes, turning minutes of polygon tracing into seconds.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Labeled masks are the bottleneck for training segmentation models (like the one in 11.2). p.354 notes that pixel-precise masks are much more time-consuming to collect than bounding boxes; SAM narrows that gap.
paragraphs.technical_idea: This is the same model-assisted labeling loop used to build SA-1B, where SAM's predictions were corrected by humans (p.343-344).

terminology.meaning: Attaching ground-truth labels (here, masks) to raw images.

connections: p.343: SA-1B was built in a feedback loop with a partially trained model.
p.354: segmentation labels cost more than detection boxes.

paragraphs.excerpt: Image segmentation is one of the main categories of computer vision
paragraphs.what_it_says: Segmentation is a main computer vision task: computing masks that describe image contents at the pixel level.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Unlike classification (one label per image) or detection (boxes), segmentation assigns information to every pixel.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Sets segmentation alongside classification and detection, the three vision tasks introduced in 11.1 and continued in chapter 12.

terminology.meaning: An image-sized array giving, for each pixel, the class or object it belongs to.

connections: p.332: chapter opener lists the branches of computer vision.
p.334: types of image segmentation (semantic, instance, panoptic).

paragraphs.excerpt: To build your own segmentation model, use a stack of strided
paragraphs.what_it_says: A from-scratch segmentation model compresses the image with strided Conv2D layers and expands it back with matching Conv2DTranspose layers to a mask the size of the input.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is an encoder-decoder: the downsampling half learns increasingly abstract features at lower resolution, and the upsampling half restores spatial resolution so each input pixel gets a prediction.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the architecture trained on the Oxford-IIIT Pets data in 11.2, producing (200, 200, 3) outputs (p.340).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Strided convolutions halve spatial size per stride-2 layer; a transposed convolution with stride 2 doubles it, so mirroring the stack restores the input size.

terminology.meaning: A learnable upsampling convolution, the spatial inverse in shape of a strided Conv2D.

connections: p.340: Conv2DTranspose stack outputs (200, 200, 3); IoU metric.

paragraphs.excerpt: You can also use a pretrained segmentation model. Segment Anything, included
paragraphs.what_it_says: A pretrained model, Segment Anything in KerasHub, can be used instead; the book says it supports image, text, point and box prompting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Pretraining at massive scale (11 million images, over 1 billion masks, p.342) lets one model segment almost anything given a prompt. Note that the chapter only explains and demonstrates point and box prompts; text and 'image' prompting are mentioned here for the first time without explanation.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mirrors the classification lesson from chapter 8: pretrained models can beat models trained from scratch, especially with little data (p.342).

terminology.meaning: Keras library of pretrained models (used to load SAM in 11.3.1).

connections: p.342: SAM introduced; analogy with pretrained classifiers in chapter 8.
p.344: the prompt can be a point or a box.

concepts.name: Box prompt
concepts.definition: A rectangle given by top-left and bottom-right corners used to tell SAM which object to segment.
concepts.intuition: A rough frame around the object.
concepts.technical: Passed as "boxes" with shape (batch, num_boxes, 2, 2) = (1, 1, 2, 2) here; no points/labels needed.
concepts.significance: Less ambiguous than a point; compatible with detector outputs.
concepts.misconception: The mask is not the box: SAM returns the object's pixels inside it, excluding apples and bowl.

concepts.name: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
concepts.definition: Pretrained promptable segmentation model from Meta AI, available in KerasHub.
concepts.technical: Image encoder + prompt encoder + mask decoder (p.344); outputs multiple candidate masks and predicted IoUs (p.348).
concepts.significance: Segments arbitrary objects without training and can bootstrap annotated datasets.
concepts.example: Peach, banana, and mango segmented in 11.3.
concepts.misconception: The chapter does not demonstrate text prompts; only points and boxes are shown.

concepts.name: Image segmentation
concepts.definition: Computing masks that describe image contents at the pixel level.
concepts.intuition: Colouring in each object or region.
concepts.technical: Output has the input's spatial size, with a class (semantic) or object id (instance) per pixel.
concepts.significance: One of the three main vision tasks with classification and detection.
concepts.example: Pet/background/outline masks in 11.2; SAM object masks in 11.3.
concepts.misconception: Segmentation is not detection: it gives exact pixels, not just a box.

concepts.name: Transposed convolution (Conv2DTranspose)
concepts.definition: A learnable upsampling layer used to expand feature maps.
concepts.intuition: The shape-wise reverse of a strided convolution.
concepts.technical: With stride 2 it doubles height and width; pairing it with strided Conv2D layers restores the input resolution.
concepts.significance: Lets a ConvNet output a full-resolution mask.
concepts.misconception: It is not the mathematical inverse of convolution; it only inverts the shape change.

concepts.name: Model-assisted annotation
concepts.definition: Using a model's predictions as a starting point that humans verify or correct when building labeled datasets.
concepts.intuition: Proofreading is faster than writing from scratch.
concepts.technical: With SAM: one click or box per object, then fix errors; used to build SA-1B (p.343-344).
concepts.significance: Cuts the main cost of segmentation datasets.
concepts.example: Prompt SAM with boxes around every fruit to label the test image.
concepts.misconception: Model output still needs checking; SAM can pick the wrong granularity (p.350).

deeper.title: Reading the boxes shape (1, 1, 2, 2)
Pretrained vs. from-scratch segmentation
deeper.body: The summary contrasts two routes. From scratch (11.2): you need a labeled dataset for your classes, train an encoder-decoder, and get a model specialised to those classes. Pretrained SAM (11.3): no training, any object, but it needs a prompt and outputs no class label. Beyond the book: a common hybrid is to use SAM to label data, then train a smaller specialised model on it, which is the dataset-creation use case mentioned on this page.

questions.question: What is the shape of the "boxes" input after ops.expand_dims(input_box, axis=(0, 1))?
questions.explanation: input_box is (2, 2); inserting size-1 axes at positions 0 and 1 gives (1, 1, 2, 2). (1, 2, 2) would be axis=0 only; (1, 4) would require flattening.

questions.question: Which input keys are passed to SAM for the box prompt?
questions.explanation: Unlike the point prompt (p.348), no "points" or "labels" are given.

questions.question: In Figure 11.15, the box includes parts of the apples, yet the mask does not. Why?
questions.answer: The box only indicates the approximate location and size of the target; SAM segments the single object the box frames, the mango, at pixel precision.
questions.explanation: SAM was trained with boxes drawn around one object's mask (p.345), so it learned to return that object, not everything in the box.

questions.question: Why does the book say SAM is useful for creating segmentation datasets?
questions.answer: Producing masks by hand is slow; SAM turns each object into a one-click or one-box task, with humans only correcting errors.
questions.explanation: Mask labels are much more costly than boxes (p.354), and SA-1B itself was built this way (p.343).

questions.question: According to the summary, which layer pair is used to build a segmentation model from scratch?
options: Strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers
questions.answer: Strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers
questions.explanation: The second summary bullet says exactly this. The other options are not the chapter's architecture.

questions.question: The summary says SAM supports text prompting. Is that supported by what the chapter showed?
questions.answer: No. The chapter explains and demonstrates only point and box prompts; text prompting is not covered.
questions.explanation: p.344 says the prompt can be a point or a box; p.347 lists only those two. Read the summary claim critically.

questions.question: Can you list, from memory, the two prompt types you used with SAM and the input keys each needs?
questions.answer: Point: images, points (1,1,2), labels (1,1). Box: images, boxes (1,1,2,2).
